tracks.name: HTML Foundations
tracks.description: Document structure, headings, paragraphs, and links.

lessons.title: 1. The HTML Document
lessons.summary: Every web page starts with a structured skeleton.

activities.title: A minimal HTML page
activities.instruction: Every HTML document follows the same pattern: a doctype declaration, an `<html>` wrapper, a `<head>` for metadata, and a `<body>` for visible content.
activities.example: Hello, world!

activities.title: What shows on screen?
activities.question: In the example above, what text will the browser actually display to the user?
choices: Both My Page and Hello, world!
activities.explanation: The `<title>` goes in the browser tab, not the page body. Only content inside `<body>` appears on the page.

teaching.text: HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. It is not a programming language — it is a markup language that tells the browser how to structure content.
Every web page begins with `<!DOCTYPE html>`. This tells the browser to use modern HTML rules. Always put it as the very first line.
Hello, world!
The `<html>` element wraps everything. Inside it, `<head>` holds information about the page (like its title), and `<body>` holds everything the user can see.
The `<title>` appears in the browser tab — not on the page itself. It is important for search engines and bookmarks.

lessons.task: Create a complete HTML document with a `<head>` containing a `<title>` reading 'My First Page', and a `<body>` containing a paragraph that says 'Welcome to HTML!'.
hints: Inside `<html>`, create a `<head>` with `<title>My First Page</title>`.

After ``, create a `` with `

Welcome to HTML!

`.
lessons.solution: Welcome to HTML!

lessons.title: 2. Headings
lessons.summary: Six levels of heading importance.

activities.title: Heading hierarchy
activities.instruction: HTML provides six heading levels. `<h1>` is the most important (usually the page title), and `<h6>` is the least important.
activities.example:
Main Title

Section

Subsection

Detail

activities.title: Which heading is largest?
activities.question: Which heading tag produces the largest text on screen?
activities.explanation: `<h1>` is the largest heading. Headings get smaller as the number increases.

teaching.text: Headings give structure to your page. Think of them like chapter titles and section headers in a book.

Main Title

Section

Subsection

Detail

Fine Detail
Smallest
Every page should have exactly **one `<h1>`** — this is the main title. Use `<h2>` for major sections, `<h3>` for subsections inside those, and so on.
Never skip heading levels. Going from `<h1>` straight to `<h4>` confuses screen readers and hurts accessibility.
Search engines use headings to understand the structure of your page. Good heading hierarchy improves your page's SEO.

lessons.task: Create a page with an `<h1>` saying 'Recipes', an `<h2>` saying 'Breakfast', and an `<h3>` saying 'Pancakes'.

lessons.title: 3. Paragraphs and Text
lessons.summary: Writing blocks of text and adding emphasis.

activities.title: Paragraphs and inline formatting
activities.instruction:
The `

` tag creates a paragraph. Inside text, `` makes bold text and `` makes italic text.
activities.example:
This is a bold word.

This is an italic word.

activities.title: Bold or strong?
activities.question: What is the difference between `<b>` and `<strong>`?
choices: No difference — they look the same
`<strong>` tells the browser the text is important, `<b>` is just visual
activities.answer: `<strong>` tells the browser the text is important, `<b>` is just visual
activities.explanation: `<strong>` carries meaning (importance), while `<b>` is purely visual. Always prefer `<strong>` for important text.

teaching.text:
The `

` tag creates a paragraph — a block of text with space above and below. Browsers treat each `

` as a separate block.

HTML is fun to learn.

It powers every website.

For inline emphasis, use `<strong>` (bold, signals importance) and `<em>` (italic, signals emphasis). These are **semantic** tags — they tell the browser *why* the text is special, not just *how* it looks.

You must not share your password.

I really like HTML.

Other useful inline tags: `

` for a horizontal rule (a dividing line), and `` for styling a chunk of text without adding meaning.

HTML ignores extra spaces and line breaks in your code. Two spaces look the same as one. Use `
` if you need a break inside a paragraph.

lessons.title: 4. Links
lessons.summary: Connecting pages together with anchor tags.

activities.title: Creating a hyperlink
activities.instruction: The `<a>` (anchor) tag creates a link. The `href` attribute specifies the destination URL.
activities.example: Visit Example

activities.title: What is clickable?
activities.question: In `Click me`, what text does the user click on?
activities.explanation: The text between the opening and closing `<a>` tags is what the user sees and clicks. The `href` value is the destination.

teaching.text: Links are the foundation of the web. Without them, pages would be islands. The `<a>` tag turns text or images into clickable links.
Visit Example
The `href` attribute stands for **Hypertext Reference** — it tells the browser where to go when the link is clicked.
Links can point to other websites, other pages on your own site, or even specific sections on the same page.
Google About Us Jump to Contact Google (new tab)
The `target="_blank"` attribute opens the link in a new tab. Always pair it with `rel="noopener noreferrer"` for security.

  <!-- Paragraph with an inline link -->
</body>
</html>
hints:
The whole thing goes in one `

` tag.

lessons.title: 5. Images
lessons.summary: Adding pictures to your page with attributes.

activities.title: An image with alt text
activities.instruction: The `` tag embeds an image. It is a **void element** — no closing tag needed. Always include an `alt` attribute describing the image.

activities.title: Why alt text?
activities.question: Why is the `alt` attribute important?
choices: It makes the image load faster
It describes the image for screen readers and when the image fails to load
activities.answer: It describes the image for screen readers and when the image fails to load
activities.explanation: Alt text is read by screen readers for visually impaired users and shown when the image cannot load.

teaching.text: The `` tag embeds an image directly into the page. It is a **void element** — it has no closing tag.
The two essential attributes are:
**`src`** (source) — the path to the image file. This can be a local file or a URL.
**`alt`** (alternative text) — a text description. Screen readers read this aloud, and browsers show it when the image fails to load. Every `` should have `alt`.
Use `width` and `height` attributes to prevent the page from jumping while images load. The values are in pixels.

tracks.name: Lists and Tables
tracks.description: Organize content with lists and structured tables.

lessons.title: 6. Unordered Lists
lessons.summary: Bullet-pointed lists for items without a specific order.

activities.title: A bulleted grocery list
activities.instruction: Use `<ul>` (unordered list) to wrap `<li>` (list item) elements. The browser displays them with bullets.
activities.example:
• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Cherries

activities.title: Bullets or numbers?
activities.question: What does a `<ul>` display its items as?
activities.explanation: `<ul>` creates a bulleted (unordered) list. Use `<ol>` for numbered (ordered) lists.

teaching.text: Unordered lists display items with bullet points. They are perfect for lists where the order does not matter — like ingredients, features, or reminders.

• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Cherries
The `<ul>` element is the container. Each `<li>` is an individual item inside it. You cannot put text directly inside `<ul>` — it must be wrapped in `<li>` tags.
Lists can be nested. Put a `<ul>` or `<ol>` inside an `<li>` to create sub-lists.

• Fruits
    • Apples
    • Bananas
  • Vegetables
    • Carrots
    • Broccoli
The default bullet style varies by browser. You can change it with CSS using `list-style-type`.

lessons.task: Create an unordered list of three programming languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
lessons.starterCode: Languages of the Web
hints: Each language goes in its own `<li>` tag.
lessons.solution:
Languages of the Web

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

lessons.title: 7. Ordered Lists
lessons.summary: Numbered lists for steps, rankings, and sequences.

activities.title: A numbered to-do list
activities.instruction: Use `<ol>` (ordered list) to create numbered items. The browser automatically numbers each `<li>`.
activities.example:
1. Wake up
  2. Brush teeth
  3. Make coffee

activities.title: Automatic numbering
activities.question: If you add a new `<li>` in the middle of an `<ol>`, what happens to the numbering?
choices: You must manually renumber all items
activities.explanation: The browser handles numbering automatically. Insert, remove, or reorder items and the numbers update.

teaching.text: Ordered lists use numbers instead of bullets. Use them for step-by-step instructions, rankings, or anything where sequence matters.

1. Wake up
  2. Brush teeth
  3. Make coffee
You can change the numbering style with the `type` attribute:

1. First
  1. First
  1. First
  1. First
The `start` attribute lets you begin numbering from a specific value:

1. Fifth
  2. Sixth
Like `<ul>`, you cannot put text directly inside `<ol>`. Every piece of content must be wrapped in an `<li>`.

lessons.task: Create an ordered list with three steps: 'Open the file', 'Edit the code', 'Save changes'.
lessons.starterCode: How to Code
hints: Use `<ol>` instead of `<ul>` for numbered steps.
Each step goes in an `<li>` tag.
lessons.solution:
How to Code

  1. Open the file
  2. Edit the code
  3. Save changes

lessons.title: 8. Tables
lessons.summary: Structuring data in rows and columns.

activities.title: A simple table
activities.instruction: Tables use `<table>` as the container, `<tr>` for rows, `<th>` for header cells (bold and centered), and `<td>` for data cells.
activities.example:
Name Age
Alice 30
Bob 25

activities.title: Header vs data cells
activities.question: What is the visual difference between `<th>` and `<td>`?
choices: `<th>` is bold and centered by default; `<td>` is plain
activities.answer: `<th>` is bold and centered by default; `<td>` is plain
activities.explanation: Browsers style `<th>` header cells as bold and centered to visually distinguish them from data cells.

teaching.text: Tables organize data into rows and columns. While they were once used for page layout, today they should only be used for actual tabular data.
The four essential tags are:

**`<table>`** — the container for the entire table.
**`<tr>`** — a table row.
**`<th>`** — a header cell (bold, centered).
**`<td>`** — a data cell (regular text).

Name Age
Alice 30
For better semantics, wrap header rows in `<thead>` and data rows in `<tbody>`:

Name Score
Alice 95
Bob 87
The `colspan` attribute lets a cell span multiple columns: `<th colspan="2">Full Name</th>`.

lessons.task: Create a table with headers 'Fruit' and 'Price', and two data rows: 'Apple' / '$1.50' and 'Banana' / '$0.75'.
hints: First `<tr>` has two `<th>` cells for headers.
Each data row uses `<tr>` with two `<td>` cells.
lessons.solution:
Fruit Prices

Fruit Price

tracks.name: Forms and Inputs
tracks.description: Collecting user data with forms, inputs, and buttons.

lessons.title: 9. Form Basics
lessons.summary: The container that wraps interactive input elements.

activities.title: A login form
activities.instruction: The `<form>` element wraps input fields and a submit button. The `action` attribute specifies where the data is sent.
activities.example:
<form action="/login" method="POST">
  <label for="user">Username:</label>
  <input type="text" id="user" name="username">

  <label for="pass">Password:</label>
  <input type="password" id="pass" name="password">

  <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

activities.title: What is method POST?
activities.question: What does `method="POST"` do on a form?
choices: Sends data in the request body (hidden from the URL)
Posts the data to social media
activities.answer: Sends data in the request body (hidden from the URL)
activities.explanation: POST sends form data in the HTTP request body, not in the URL. GET appends data to the URL as query parameters.

teaching.text: A form is a container for input elements. When the user clicks Submit, the browser collects the data and sends it somewhere.
Two important attributes on `<form>`:

**`action`** — the URL where form data is sent.
**`method`** — how the data is sent (`GET` puts it in the URL, `POST` hides it in the request body).

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <input type="text" name="query">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>
The `name` attribute on each input is crucial — it becomes the key in the submitted data. Without `name`, the input's value is not sent.
Every `<label>` should have a `for` attribute matching the `id` of its input. This makes the label clickable and improves accessibility.

lessons.task: Create a form with `action="/signup"` and `method="POST"`. Inside, add a text input named `email` with a label 'Email:', and a submit button labeled 'Sign Up'.
hints: Add a `<label for="email">Email:</label>` and `<input type="text" id="email" name="email">`.
lessons.solution: Sign Up

lessons.title: 10. Input Types
lessons.summary: Text, email, password, number, checkbox, radio, and more.

activities.title: Different input types
activities.instruction: The `<input>` tag changes behavior based on its `type` attribute. Each type provides the right keyboard and validation for its purpose.
activities.example:
<input type="text" placeholder="Your name">
<input type="email" placeholder="you@email.com">
<input type="password" placeholder="Secret">
<input type="number" min="0" max="100">
<input type="checkbox" id="agree">
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="free"> Free

activities.title: Type behavior
activities.question: What happens when a user types 'hello' in an `<input type="email">` and tries to submit?
choices: The browser shows a validation error
activities.answer: The browser shows a validation error
activities.explanation: Browsers validate `type="email"` inputs — they must contain an @ symbol. Invalid values trigger a built-in error message.

teaching.text: The `<input>` element is the most versatile form element. Its `type` attribute determines what kind of data it collects and how it behaves.
Common input types:

<!-- Plain text -->
<input type="text" name="name">

<!-- Email (browser validates @) -->
<input type="email" name="email">

<!-- Password (hides characters) -->
<input type="password" name="password">

<!-- Number (shows spinner, validates) -->
<input type="number" name="age" min="0" max="120">

<!-- Date picker -->
<input type="date" name="birthday">
For choices, use checkboxes and radio buttons:

<!-- Checkbox: can select multiple -->
<input type="checkbox" id="newsletter" name="newsletter" value="yes">
<label for="newsletter">Subscribe to newsletter</label>

<!-- Radio: can select only one (same name = same group) -->
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" id="free">
<label for="free">Free</label>
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro" id="pro">
<label for="pro">Pro</label>
Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group — only one can be selected. Checkboxes are independent.
The `placeholder` attribute shows hint text inside the input before the user types. The `required` attribute makes the field mandatory.

lessons.task: Create a form with: a text input (name='username'), a password input (name='password'), and a checkbox with label 'Remember me'.
hints: For the checkbox: `<input type="checkbox" id="remember"> <label for="remember">Remember me</label>`.
lessons.solution: Login

lessons.title: 11. Dropdowns and Text Areas
lessons.summary: Dropdown menus and multi-line text input.

activities.title: A dropdown and a text area
activities.instruction: The `<select>` element creates a dropdown menu with `<option>` items. The `<textarea>` creates a multi-line text box.
activities.example:
<select name="color">
  <option value="red">Red</option>
  <option value="blue">Blue</option>
  <option value="green">Green</option>
</select>

<textarea name="bio" rows="5" cols="40">Tell us about yourself...</textarea>

activities.title: Option values
activities.question: When the user selects 'Blue' in the dropdown, what value is submitted?
activities.explanation: The `value` attribute is what gets submitted. The text between `<option>` tags is what the user sees.

teaching.text: For dropdown menus, use `<select>` with `<option>` children. Each option has a `value` attribute — this is what gets submitted to the server.

<select name="country">
  <option value="us">United States</option>
  <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
  <option value="jp">Japan</option>
</select>
You can pre-select an option with the `selected` attribute:
<option value="uk" selected>United Kingdom</option>
For longer text input, use `<textarea>` instead of `<input>`. It supports multiple lines and can be resized by the user.

<textarea name="message" rows="6" cols="50" placeholder="Write your message...">
</textarea>
`rows` and `cols` set the initial size. The user can usually drag to resize, which you can control with CSS.

lessons.task: Create a form with a `<select>` dropdown named 'plan' with three options ('Free', 'Pro', 'Enterprise'), and a `<textarea>` named 'message' with 4 rows.
lessons.starterCode: Contact Us
hints: Each option needs a `value` attribute and display text.
lessons.solution: Contact Us

tracks.name: Semantic HTML
tracks.description: Meaningful tags that describe your content's purpose.

lessons.title: 12. Why Semantic HTML Matters
lessons.summary: Using the right tag for the right job.

activities.title: Div soup vs semantic HTML
activities.instruction: Semantic tags like `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, and `<footer>` describe the purpose of content. Compare this with using `<div>` for everything.
activities.example:
...

Post Title

Content...

...

activities.title: Why not just use divs?
activities.question: What is the main advantage of semantic tags over `<div>`?
choices: They convey meaning to browsers, screen readers, and search engines
activities.answer: They convey meaning to browsers, screen readers, and search engines
activities.explanation: Semantic tags don't change the visual appearance much, but they communicate the *role* of each section to assistive technology and search engines.

teaching.text: Semantic HTML means using tags that describe the **meaning** of content, not just its appearance.
The key semantic layout tags are:

<header>    — introductory content or navigation bar
<nav>        — navigation links
<main>       — the main content of the page
<article>    — self-contained content (blog post, news story)
<section>    — a thematic grouping of content
<aside>      — tangentially related content (sidebar)
<footer>     — footer information (copyright, links)
A typical page layout looks like this:

Home About

My Blog Post

Today I learned about semantic HTML...

Related: CSS Basics

© 2026 My Website
Screen readers use semantic tags to help visually impaired users navigate a page. Using `<nav>` tells them 'this section contains navigation links'.

lessons.title: 13. Block vs Inline Elements
lessons.summary: Understanding how elements flow on the page.

activities.title: Block vs inline behavior
activities.instruction: Block elements (`div`, `p`, `h1`-`h6`, `ul`, `table`) start on a new line and take the full width. Inline elements (`span`, `a`, `strong`, `em`, `img`) flow within the text.
activities.example:

Second paragraph

I am bold and italic text.

activities.title: Block stacking
activities.question: Two `<div>` elements will appear as:
choices: Side by side on the same line
Stacked vertically, one on top of the other
activities.answer: Stacked vertically, one on top of the other
activities.explanation: Block elements always start on a new line and occupy the full available width, so they stack vertically.

teaching.text: HTML elements fall into two display categories: **block** and **inline**.
**Block elements** start on a new line and stretch to fill the available width:

,

**Inline elements** do not start a new line. They flow within the surrounding text:

, , , , ,

The `<div>` is a generic block container — it has no meaning by itself, so use semantic tags instead when possible. The `<span>` is the inline equivalent.

This paragraph is inside a div.

This paragraph is also inside the same div.

This paragraph is red text in a sentence.
You can change an element's display behavior with CSS: `display: inline` or `display: block`.

lessons.title: 14. Details, Figures, and Other Semantics
lessons.summary: Built-in interactive and semantic elements.

activities.title: A collapsible section
activities.instruction: The `<details>` element creates a disclosure widget that the user can open and close. The `<summary>` inside it is the visible label.
activities.example:
Click to expand

Here is the hidden content that appears when you click.

activities.title: No JavaScript needed!
activities.question: Does the `<details>` element require JavaScript to open and close?
choices: Yes, you need JS to toggle it
No, the browser handles it natively
activities.answer: No, the browser handles it natively
activities.explanation: The `<details>` element is a native HTML disclosure widget — no JavaScript required. It works in all modern browsers.

teaching.text: HTML has several powerful semantic elements that also provide built-in functionality:

Click to expand

The `<figure>` element wraps self-contained content like images, code blocks, or diagrams. Use `<figcaption>` for the caption:
The `<blockquote>` element marks a quotation from another source:
The best way to learn HTML is to practice.
Other useful semantic tags:
HTML highlighted text deleted text inserted text inline code
The `<abbr>` tag is great for accessibility — screen readers can announce the full form when available.

tracks.name: Media and Embedding
tracks.description: Audio, video, iframes, and embedding external content.

lessons.title: 15. Audio and Video
lessons.summary: Embedding multimedia content directly in your page.

activities.title: A video player
activities.instruction: The `<video>` tag embeds a video with built-in playback controls. The `<source>` element specifies the file and format.
activities.example:
<video controls width="640">
  <source src="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <source src="movie.webm" type="video/webm">
  Your browser does not support video.
</video>

activities.title: Fallback text
activities.question: What does the text 'Your browser does not support video.' do?
choices: It only appears if the browser cannot play the video
activities.answer: It only appears if the browser cannot play the video
activities.explanation: Content inside `<video>` (outside `<source>`) is fallback content — only shown if the browser cannot handle the element.

teaching.text: The `<video>` and `<audio>` elements embed media directly in your page with native browser controls.

<!-- Video with controls -->
<video controls width="640" height="360">
  <source src="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <source src="movie.webm" type="video/webm">
  Your browser does not support video.
</video>

<!-- Audio with controls -->
<audio controls>
  <source src="song.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <source src="song.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  Your browser does not support audio.
</audio>
The `controls` attribute adds play, pause, and volume buttons. Without it, the media plays but has no visible controls.
Other useful attributes:

**`autoplay`** — starts playing automatically (often blocked by browsers).
**`loop`** — replays when finished.
**`muted`** — starts muted (required for autoplay in most browsers).
**`poster`** — an image shown before the video plays.
Always provide at least two source formats (like MP4 and WebM) for wider browser compatibility.

lessons.task: Add a `<video>` element with `controls` and `width="480"`. Include one `<source>` pointing to 'demo.mp4' with type 'video/mp4'. Add fallback text 'Video not supported.'.
hints: Add fallback text before the closing `</video>`.
lessons.solution: Demo Video

lessons.title: 16. Iframes — Embedding External Content
lessons.summary: Displaying another webpage inside your page.

activities.title: Embedding a map
activities.instruction: The `<iframe>` element embeds another HTML document inside the current page. Commonly used for maps, videos, and third-party widgets.
activities.example:
<iframe
  src="https://www.example.com"
  width="600"
  height="400"
  title="Example website"
  loading="lazy"
></iframe>

activities.title: Security boundary
activities.question: Can JavaScript inside an iframe access the parent page's content?
choices: Only if both pages are on the same domain (same-origin policy)
activities.answer: Only if both pages are on the same domain (same-origin policy)
activities.explanation: The same-origin policy prevents cross-origin iframes from accessing the parent. Same-domain iframes have more access.

teaching.text: An `<iframe>` (inline frame) embeds another webpage inside your current page. The browser loads the external URL in a separate browsing context.

<iframe
  src="https://www.example.com"
  width="600"
  height="400"
  title="Description of the embedded content"
  loading="lazy"
></iframe>
The `title` attribute is required for accessibility — screen readers use it to describe the embedded content.
The `loading="lazy"` attribute tells the browser to defer loading until the iframe is about to enter the viewport — this improves page performance.
Common iframe use cases: embedded maps, YouTube videos, payment forms, and third-party widgets.
Iframes can be a security risk. Never embed untrusted content without the `sandbox` attribute, which restricts what the embedded page can do.

lessons.task: Embed an iframe pointing to 'https://example.com' with `width="500"`, `height="300"`, and a `title` saying 'Example page'.

tracks.name: Advanced HTML

lessons.title: 17. The Head — Meta Tags and SEO
lessons.summary: Information that search engines and browsers need.

activities.title: A complete head section
activities.instruction: The `<head>` contains metadata — information about the page, not visible content. Key elements include `<meta>` tags and `<link>` tags.
activities.example:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="A guide to HTML">
  <title>HTML Guide</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>

activities.title: Viewport meta tag
activities.question: What does `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` do?
choices: Makes the page responsive on mobile devices
activities.answer: Makes the page responsive on mobile devices
activities.explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to set the page width to the device width and start at 100% zoom, enabling responsive design.

teaching.text: The `<head>` section contains metadata that browsers, search engines, and social media platforms use to understand your page.

<head>
  <!-- Character encoding (always include) -->
  <meta charset="UTF-8">

  <!-- Responsive design (always include) -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

  <!-- SEO description -->
  <meta name="description" content="A beginner guide to HTML">

  <!-- Page title (shows in browser tab) -->
  <title>HTML Guide</title>

  <!-- Link to CSS -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
For social media sharing, add Open Graph tags:

<meta property="og:title" content="HTML Guide">
<meta property="og:description" content="Learn HTML from scratch">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/preview.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/html-guide">
The `charset="UTF-8"` meta tag should always be the first thing in your `<head>`. It ensures special characters display correctly.
Good meta descriptions improve click-through rates from search engine results. Keep them under 160 characters.

lessons.task: Create a complete `<head>` with: charset UTF-8, viewport meta tag, a description meta tag saying 'My awesome website', and a title 'My Site'.
hints: Add the viewport and description meta tags.
Finish with `<title>My Site</title>` and close with `</head>`.
lessons.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>

<head>

  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="My awesome website">
  <title>My Site</title>
</head>
<body>
</body>
</html>

lessons.title: 18. HTML Entities and Special Characters
lessons.summary: Writing characters that have special meaning in HTML.

activities.title: Escaping special characters
activities.instruction: Some characters have special meaning in HTML (like `<` and `>` for tags). To display them as text, use entity references.
activities.example:
Use <div> to create a container.

Tom & Jerry is a classic show.

The symbol © represents copyright.

activities.title: Entity display
activities.question: What does `&` display as on screen?
activities.explanation: `&` is the HTML entity for the ampersand character `&`. It displays as a single `&` on the page.

teaching.text: HTML reserves `<`, `>`, `&`, and double quotes for markup purposes. To display these characters as text, you must use **HTML entities**.

<!-- Less than -->
<   displays as: <

<!-- Greater than -->
>   displays as: >

<!-- Ampersand -->
&  displays as: &

<!-- Quotation mark -->
" displays as: "
You can also use entity references for special symbols:

©   → ©   (copyright)
®    → ®   (registered)
™  → ™   (trademark)
€   → €   (euro)
£  → £   (pound)
¥    → ¥   (yen)
    →     (non-breaking space)
The most common entity is ` ` (non-breaking space). It prevents the browser from collapsing whitespace or breaking at that point.

Hello World

Hello   World
Inside `<code>` or `<pre>` blocks, browsers preserve whitespace, so you may not need ` ` there.

lessons.title: 19. Data Attributes and IDs
lessons.summary: Storing custom data and identifying elements.

activities.title: Custom data on elements
activities.instruction: Data attributes let you store custom information on any HTML element. They start with `data-` and can be read with JavaScript.
activities.example: Admin User

activities.title: Where does custom data go?
activities.question: Can data attributes be placed on any HTML element?
activities.explanation: Data attributes are universal — you can add them to any HTML element: divs, paragraphs, images, buttons, etc.

teaching.text: Every HTML element can have an `id` (unique identifier) and `class` (shared label for CSS/JS). These are the most common attributes.

Title

Welcome!
**IDs** must be unique on the page — only one element can have a given ID. They are used for direct targeting and for `<label for="...">` connections.
**Classes** can be shared by multiple elements. They are the primary way to apply CSS styles and group elements for JavaScript.
**Data attributes** (`data-*`) store custom data on elements. They are read by JavaScript with `element.dataset`.
• JavaScript Basics
Keep IDs lowercase with hyphens (like `main-header`), not camelCase or underscores.

lessons.title: 20. Accessibility Basics
lessons.summary: Making your pages usable by everyone.

activities.title: Accessible form
activities.instruction: Accessibility means making your site usable by everyone, including people with disabilities. Screen readers, keyboard navigation, and proper labels are key.
activities.example: Type a keyword to search the site.

activities.title: What does aria-describedby do?
activities.question: What does the `aria-describedby` attribute do?
choices: Links the input to a description that screen readers will read
activities.answer: Links the input to a description that screen readers will read
activities.explanation: `aria-describedby` points to an element whose text is read by screen readers as additional description of the current element.

teaching.text: Web accessibility (often abbreviated a11y) ensures your content is usable by people with visual, motor, auditory, or cognitive disabilities.
HTML gives you many built-in accessibility features:

Page Title

Section

Subsection

Navigation
Main content
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes add extra information when HTML alone is not enough:

New message received
Decorative only
The first rule of ARIA: use native HTML elements when possible. Only add ARIA attributes when HTML alone cannot convey the right semantics.
